data.text:
I searched each claim. Source quality varies, and I note this where it matters.

**Claim 0: Suburban turning circle of about 39 ft (about 12 m). Not supported. Corrected: about 42–43 ft (about 13 m).**
- GM Authority's 2024 Suburban spec sheet lists a turning circle of 42.3 ft / 12.9 m with 18-inch wheels, and 43.3 ft / 13.2 m with 20- and 22-inch wheels. https://gmauthority.com/blog/gm/chevrolet/suburban/2024-chevrolet-suburban/2024-chevrolet-suburban-specifications/ (GM Authority is a trade site that reproduces GM's published specs.)
- KBB's 2026 specs list a turning diameter of 41.5 feet on the first two trims and 43.3 feet on the rest. https://www.kbb.com/chevrolet/suburban/2026/specs/
- I found no source giving 39 ft. The figure is about 3–4 ft too small, and 12 m is closer to 13 m. For the script, use "about 43 feet, roughly 13 meters."

**Claim 1: Mercedes S-Class rear steering turns up to 10° and cuts the turning circle by up to about 2 m. Supported as written.**
- Mercedes' own S-Class (W223) material, quoted on a forum thread, says the turning circle is reduced by up to 2 metres with rear-axle steering compared to a model without it, and the maximum steering angle is 10°. It also says that even the long-wheelbase S-Class gets a turning circle under 11 metres. https://www.germancarforum.com/threads/official-mercedes-benz-s-class-w223.60931/page-6 (This is a forum repost of the press text, so it is secondary.)
- Autoevolution says the turning circle is decreased by 6.5 feet (2 meters), giving roughly the same turning circle as the much smaller A-Class. https://www.autoevolution.com/news/mercedes-benz-revolutionizes-rear-wheel-steering-in-the-2021-s-class-149535.html
- Two versions exist. The 10° system is the larger one, and a 4.5° version is based on existing technology. Say "optional" and "up to 10°."

**Claim 2: Rear wheels steer opposite the front at low speed and the same way at higher speed, with the switch at about 60 km/h. Partly supported. The principle is correct, but 60 km/h is not a universal figure.**
- Motor Authority, on the S-Class, says that at low speeds the rear wheels move opposite to the front wheels, and at higher speeds front and rear turn in unison for stability. https://www.motorauthority.com/news/1129048_mercedes-adds-improved-active-body-control-and-rear-wheel-steering-to-new-s-class
- Autoevolution's explainer on BMW-style integral steering says under 60 km/h the wheels steer in opposing directions, and above 80 km/h they turn in the same direction. https://www.autoevolution.com/news/integral-steering-system-explained-20848.html That gives a transition band, not a single switch point at 60.
- Porsche's Taycan figure, quoted on a forum, is opposite-direction steering at speeds up to about 50 km/h, with a maximum of 2.8 degrees. https://www.taycanforum.com/forum/threads/rear-axle-steering.1440/page-3 (Forum source, so treat it as weak.) The threshold therefore varies by manufacturer.
- Corrected wording: "At low speeds, roughly below 50–60 km/h depending on the car, the rear wheels steer opposite the front. At higher speeds they steer the same way." I found no Mercedes figure for the S-Class switch speed.

**Claim 3: The GMC Hummer EV's CrabWalk turns all four wheels the same way so the truck drives diagonally. Supported, with a caveat about angle and speed.**
- Cars.com says CrabWalk allows all four wheels to be turned in the same direction up to a 10-degree angle. https://www.cars.com/articles/what-is-the-gmc-hummer-evs-crabwalk-feature-443574/
- A GMC dealer's explainer says that at low speeds or stopped, you can turn all four wheels in unison up to 10 degrees, so the Hummer crawls diagonally like a crab. https://www.cochranbuickgmcyoungstown.com/blog/what-is-the-hummer-ev-crab-walk/ (Dealer source, so it is secondary.) I did not find the GMC press page itself.
- Add "at low speed, up to 10°." The truck moves diagonally at a modest angle, not sideways.

**Other points for the script**
- Claim 1 supports the "like a compact" framing. Mercedes says the S-Class gets turning circle under 11 metres. The Mercedes C-Class, a smaller car, gets 11.2 m (37 ft) with 4.5° rear steering, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_C-Class_with_EQ_Technology).
- Do not pair the S-Class with the Suburban figure as if the same system were fitted. The S-Class system is a Mercedes option, not something the Suburban has.
